prayer.text: Saint Hedwig of Silesia, pray for us.

cues.text: A Bavarian Noblewoman
Born around 1174 at the castle of Andechs in Bavaria, Hedwig was one of eight children of Count Berthold IV.
His family connections spread across medieval Europe's ruling houses.
Her sister Gertrude's daughter would become St. Elizabeth of Hungary , making Hedwig that beloved saint's aunt.
Educated at the monastery of Kitzingen, Hedwig was married at only twelve years old to Henry I , Duke of Silesia, in what is now southwestern Poland.
A Devout Ducal Household

Hedwig and Henry built a genuinely pious and productive marriage, raising seven children together and jointly founding monasteries, hospitals, and charitable institutions across Silesia, including the great Cistercian convent at Trebnitz .
Even as duchess, Hedwig lived with notable personal austerity, practicing severe self-denial and devoting herself to prayer and works of mercy for the poor and the sick.
A Peacemaker in War
When her husband was captured during a conflict with Duke Conrad of Masovia in 1229, Hedwig personally traveled to intercede on his behalf.
Her appearance and evident holiness so moved Conrad that he released Henry from captivity—an early instance of the diplomatic influence her reputation for sanctity carried even among rival rulers.
Loss and Widowhood
Of her seven children, only her daughter Gertrude, who became abbess of Trebnitz, outlived her; her son Duke Henry II died in 1241 fighting the invading Mongols at the Battle of Legnica.
After her husband Henry I's death in 1238, Hedwig took the grey habit of the Cistercians at Trebnitz.
She declined formal profession as a nun so that she might retain control of her considerable resources for continued charitable use.
Final Years of Charity

In her widowhood, Hedwig continued and expanded her charitable work, ministering personally to prisoners and to those afflicted with leprosy, and living, by all contemporary accounts, a life of remarkable humility and self-denial despite her rank.
She died at Trebnitz in 1243, already regarded during her lifetime, in the words of the Catholic Encyclopedia, with 'the reputation of a saint.'
Legacy
Hedwig was canonized by Pope Clement IV in 1267 and remains one of the most beloved patron saints of Silesia, Poland, and Germany alike.
She is venerated today as patroness of widows, orphans, and refugees.
Throughout her life, her vast wealth and status, as a duchess, became instruments for relieving the poor and suffering rather than ends in themselves.
